findings.summary: Firewall rule allow-ssh-from-iap (priority 1000, explicit ALLOW) permits inbound tcp/22 from 35.235.240.0/20, which contains source 35.235.240.5, targeting instances tagged ssh-allowed, including app-server-1's nic0. This explicit rule outranks GCP's implied deny-ingress default rule (priority 65534).

evidence.detail: direction=INGRESS, action=ALLOW, priority=1000, sourceRanges=[35.235.240.0/20], allowed=[{IPProtocol:tcp,ports:[22]}], targetTags=[ssh-allowed]

reasoning.description: 35.235.240.5 is contained within source range 35.235.240.0/20, permitted by allow-ssh-from-iap.
allow-ssh-from-iap's priority 1000 is numerically lower (higher precedence) than GCP's implied deny-ingress default rule at priority 65534, so the explicit ALLOW wins for this traffic.

assumptions: app-server-1 carries the ssh-allowed network tag targeted by this rule.

findings.summary: Traffic sourced from the IAP range additionally requires the connecting principal to hold the roles/iam.tunnelResourceAccessor IAM binding (or equivalent) and to pass Identity-Aware Proxy's own per-request TCP-forwarding authorization; this collection has no IAM policy binding data in scope to evaluate that layer, so whether a specific caller can actually open the tunnel cannot be determined here.
limitations: IAM policy bindings for roles/iam.tunnelResourceAccessor were not collected as part of this path evaluation; this finding cannot confirm whether the specific calling principal is authorized to open an IAP TCP-forwarding tunnel to this instance, only that the VPC firewall layer permits the traffic once IAP has forwarded it.
